anchor: Plan v27 Lane C.5 — hand-picked city-vs-city comparison pairs. Canonical slug format: alphabetically-first-vs-alphabetically-second (e.g., new-york-vs-san-francisco, not san-francisco-vs-new-york). Each pair has a one-sentence editorial hook.
convention: left and right are city slugs from city_list_v1.json. The pair's URL is /compare/cities/{left}-vs-{right} — verify alphabetical order before adding new pairs.

pairs.hook: Two financial capitals on opposite sides of the Atlantic. London is older and denser, New York is bigger and richer per resident.
America's two biggest metros. New York stacks vertically and concentrates finance; Los Angeles sprawls horizontally and concentrates creative industries.
The world's two software supercities. San Francisco is a smaller, denser, older market with deeper venture infrastructure; Shenzhen is younger, larger, and tightly coupled to manufacturing.
East Asia's two most concentrated metros. Tokyo is much larger by population; Seoul runs hotter on tech adoption and consumer services.
Europe's two cultural capitals. Paris is wealthier per capita and tighter on real estate; Berlin is cheaper, larger by area, and tilts toward creative SMBs.
India's two megacities. Mumbai is the financial capital; Delhi is the political and administrative center with a more diverse industrial base.
The two top trade-and-finance hubs of the eastern hemisphere. Singapore is tightly regulated and services-heavy; Dubai is tourist-and-trade-heavy with broader retail.
Latin America's two biggest metros. São Paulo runs Brazil's industrial economy; Mexico City anchors both finance and a large informal SMB sector.
Canada's two coastal anchors. Toronto is the larger financial hub; Vancouver runs higher per-capita wealth and tilts toward natural-resource trade.
Spain's two largest metros. Madrid is the political and corporate center; Barcelona runs heavier on tourism, design, and Mediterranean trade.
Southeast Asia's two big trade cities. Bangkok is older, larger, and more tourist-anchored; Ho Chi Minh City is younger and faster-growing on manufacturing.
Africa's two main commercial capitals. Lagos is much larger and oil-anchored; Nairobi is smaller, wealthier per capita, and more services-heavy.
Two ancient capitals straddling the Mediterranean. Istanbul is wealthier and more industrially diverse; Cairo is larger by population with a heavier informal economy.
South America's two southern-cone capitals. Buenos Aires is bigger; Santiago is wealthier per capita and runs cleaner governance.
Australia's two biggest cities. Sydney is the financial capital; Melbourne is culturally heavier and slightly larger by population.
Two Chinese-speaking financial cities. Hong Kong is denser and more global-finance-anchored; Taipei is wealthier per capita on hardware and software.
Two northwest European capitals an hour apart. Brussels runs on EU institutions; Amsterdam runs on trade, tourism, and creative industries.
Two large Slavic capitals. Moscow is much larger and resource-anchored; Warsaw is smaller, faster-growing, and integrated with the EU economy.
Southeast Asia's two megacity capitals. Jakarta is the bigger metro economy; Manila is denser per square kilometer and more services-heavy.
Two Gulf capitals. Riyadh is much larger; Doha runs richer per capita on a tighter gas-anchored base.
